lesson.title: A Second Pair of Eyes: What Code Review Catches
lesson.summary: Code review is peer examination of code before it is merged, checking it for correctness and maintainability rather than just style.
lesson.body:
So far, every technique in this unit is something you can do alone: writing tests first, tracing code by hand, using a debugger, even explaining code to a rubber duck. Code review is different. It means having another person examine your code, typically before it is merged into the shared codebase, checking it for correctness and for maintainability, meaning how easy it will be for someone else to read, understand, and safely change later, not just whether it follows a formatting style.

The reason this catches things that solo techniques miss is simple: you already know what your code is supposed to do, which makes it easy to read past a mistake because your brain fills in the intention rather than seeing what is actually written. A reviewer has no such blind spot. They read the code fresh, with no memory of writing it, which means they notice things the author has stopped seeing, missing edge cases, confusing names, logic that works for the one case the author tested but not for others.

This builds on both testing and code readability. A reviewer typically checks whether tests exist for the change and whether those tests actually cover the interesting cases, not just the easy ones, since a change with no tests, or tests that only check the happy path, is much more likely to hide a bug. A reviewer also evaluates readability directly: whether variable and function names describe what they hold or do, whether the logic is organized in a way a stranger could follow six months from now, and whether complexity has been introduced that is not actually needed to solve the problem.

Consider this function, submitted for review:

def get_discounted_price(price, discount):
    return price - price * discount

A reviewer might leave a comment like this: "What happens if discount is passed as 20, meaning twenty percent, instead of 0.2? This returns a negative price with no error at all, since nothing here checks the range of discount. Should the parameter be renamed to discount_fraction to make the expected unit clear, or should there be a check that raises an error if discount is outside 0 to 1? Also, I do not see a test for discount equal to 0 or discount equal to 1, both are reasonable edge cases worth covering." Nothing here is a style nitpick. The reviewer found a correctness problem, a function that produces a plausible looking but wrong number for a certain kind of bad input, exactly the sort of silent failure that automated tests will only catch if someone thought to write that specific test case, and exactly the sort of thing an author, focused on the discount math working for the input they tried, is likely to read straight past.

Good code review is not about proving the author wrong. It is a second, independent check on correctness and clarity, the same goals as testing and readability individually, applied by someone whose fresh perspective is itself the tool.
